This is the portion of the meeting set aside for general public comment directly related to City business, for matters that do 
not appear on this evening’s agenda. If you are here for a specific agenda item that is under Unfinished Business or New 
Business, please wait until we reach that item. Items under First Reading & Referral will be discussed when they return 
under Unfinished Business, and we will hear public comment at that time.  Public comment requires a person to state your 
name and whether you are a resident of Bangor. The City Council has adopted a Public Comment Policy that we will 
adhere to. Statements during public comment should respect the dignity and seriousness of the proceeding, and individuals 
will be restricted to speaking once. Obscene, truly threatening, or overly repetitive comments will be deemed out of order 
and will be interrupted and removed. Topics that are considered out of order also include matters that are in litigation, 
individual employees or employee groups discussing matters for which complaint or grievance procedures are in place, 
personal disputes between the speaker and another resident not germane to City business, support for or opposition to any 
candidate for political office, and personnel complaints pertaining to individual City employees. There is a time limit of 
three minutes per speaker, and the total time allowed for general public comment regarding City business will be limited to 
no more than one hour. The public comment period is for City Council members to listen and not to respond or debate 
with persons. If you do not live in Bangor or own property in Bangor, please allow those who do to have the opportunity to 
speak first. If you’d like to offer comment on any item directly related to City business not appearing on the regular 
agenda, you may approach the podium. Individuals who have appropriately pre-registered to give public comment via 
remote means will be given the opportunity to participate remotely. Alternatively, Councilors may be reached via email

Executive Summary: This Order will authorize the execution of a construction contract with C&C Lynch

This work is intended to lay a portion of the new sewer main along the northeast edge of the property 
located at 773 Stillwater from the existing sewer main servicing the Bangor Mall located on the south side

within the City's time frame. Funding for this work will be primarily through ARPA funding which 
requires work be completed by end of calendar year 2026.  Additional funding of approximately $15,000 
will be provided from local funds approved in the 2027 fiscal year Wastewater Budget.

Attachment 2 - Schedule A, Urban Developed Area to 
Remove Floor Area Ratio from the Downtown 
Development District (First Reading and Referral to 
Planning Board meeting on October 20, 2026) 
MALLAR 
    
Executive Summary: This Ordinance amendment would remove Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from the Downtown 
Development District (DDD) to provide flexibility for growth in downtown and promote infill development. 
Floor area ratio is the floor area of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. 
 
FAR was used to control building bulk and volume in the early to mid-20th century. When FARs were 
implemented around the country, some of the perceived benefits were protecting sunlight, neighborhood 
character, and infrastructure capacity, most of which do not hold true today. Additionally, some of the most 
well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For example, the Graham Building where 
the Rudman Winchell offices are located have a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the Eastern Trust building at 6 
State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
 
The proposed amendments align with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations. 
    
26-294 RESOLVE Accepting and Appropriating $823,851 for the Nourish 
ME Rural Nutrition Education Program From the 
University of New England (First Reading) 
DEANE 
    
Executive Summary: This Resolve will accept and appropriate $823,851 from the University of New 
England (UNE) to implement the Nourish ME nutrition education program in fiscal years 2027 and 2028 
in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties. 
 
Maine's Rural Health Transformation Program provides the funds for the Nourish ME program statewide, 
which focuses on reducing the burden of chronic illness through nutrition.  
 
Bangor Public Health and Community Services implemented SNAP Ed programming from 2012 - 2025. 
Federal funding for the SNAP Education program was ended nationally on February 28, 2026. In response, 
Maine DHHS dedicated new federal Rural Health Transformation Program funding to nutrition education. 
UNE is the implementing agency for the program.  
 
Funding is for a five-year program with year one funding beginning May 1, 2026. This funding allows an 
important program to continue operating despite the loss of federal funding.   
 
In FY25, Bangor Public Health and Community Services SNAP Ed nutrition educators provided nutrition 
education to 3,057 youth in 25 schools, and 266 adults in Penobscot and Piscataquis counties. The program 
helped teach participants how to stretch food dollars and make healthy choices.

26-295 RESOLVE Accepting and Appropriating Up to $6,000 from Johns 
Hopkins University as Partners on a National Institutes 
for Health ARISE Grant to Increase Access to PrEP 
(First Reading and Referral to Government Operations 
Committee Meeting on October 19, 2026) 
WALKER 
    
Executive Summary: This Order will accept and appropriate up to $6,000 from Johns Hopkins University 
as partners on a National Institutes for Health (NIH) ARISE grant to increase access to PrEP. 
 
For the past year, Bangor Public Health and Community Services has been exploring opportunities to 
expand access to Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP). PrEP is an effective medication to prevent the 
transmission of HIV. The current HIV outbreak has revealed gaps in access to PrEP. It is often not offered 
through traditional primary care. As a result, other delivery models need to be established. Bangor Public 
Health and Community Services currently has two clinic locations that could offer PrEP services. In 
addition to meeting a community need, this would also be a billable service to contribute to the 
Department's revenue. 
 
The NIH ARISE grant will bring together Johns Hopkins University's expertise and leadership with 
Bangor Public Health and Community Service's on the ground experience to create a plan to include 
increase access to PrEP through community partnerships and system building. The funding will be used to 
offset staff time to work on developing the plan and expenses for supporting community meeting logistics.

MEETING MINUTES 
 
City Councilors Present: Leonard, Faloon, Mallar, Carson, Deane, Hawes 
 
City Staff Present: Krieg, Collette, Maquillan 
 
Chair Leonard called the meeting to order at 7:18 P.M.  
 
 
1. Report of the Airport 
 
Chair Leonard introduced the agenda item. 
 
Airport Director Saavedra presented an end of year report , discussing the 2025 Annual 
Report. He shared that despite disruptions due to runway construction, the airport 
experienced a strong year. Saavedra discussed the financial year figures and the 
enterprise fund.  
 
Chair Leonard asked what the asset for the City’s airport is going into the future and the 
capabilities for growth. Airport Director Saavedra discussed the business relationship with 
the military and its contribution to revenue. Saavedra shared that fostering that relationship 
by visiting facilities and encouraging use of Bangor is an opportunity for continued growth. 
He discussed increases in domestic airline passengers and collaborating with airlines to 
incorporate strategies.  Saavedra noted the airport’s ability to service private aircrafts 
efficiently. He discussed potential cultivation with cargo expansions.  
 
Chair Leonard asked whether there are other capacities the airport could potentially grow 
and expand on, but did not have the staff to collect data on. Airport Director Saavedra 
responded that he believes there is more growth to be done in each of the outl ined 
segments before exploring other options. Leonard responded that networking with other 
industries will be apart of growth, and asked what limitations the airport may encounter in 
networking with other entities. Saavedra responded that since the airport is a department 
under the City’s jurisdiction, guidance on the direction of the airport and the amount of 
resources allocated comes from the Committee and Council. Saavedra discussed the 
importance of setting up structures that foster development and empowers growth of the 
airport.  
 
Councilor Carson expressed that he would like to see a future discussion surrounding a 
commission related to the airport and the procurement policy. He discussed wanting to 
hear the specific challenges the airport faces related to municipal policy. Chair Leonard 
asked Airport Director Saavedra if that is something he could prepare for the Committee. 
Saavedra clarified that there would be a discussion about challenges with policy, and a 
conversation about options of oversight and structure.  
 
 
2. Proposed Changes to Land Development Code – State Statute Changes
Chair Leonard introduced the agenda item. 
 
Planning Officer Collette discussed the state laws requiring changes to the City’s code 
and drafted changes to address compliance. She presented on the changes to Accessory 
Dwelling Unit allowance, additional height allowance and reduced parking requiremen ts 
for affordable housing, and units per lot minimum and minimum lot size in urban zones.  
 
Councilor Deane asked if 14 feet is two stories – Planning Officer Collette responded it is 
likely an extra story on top of what is already allowed. Deane asked how many stories are 
currently allowed – Collette provided an overview of the different district requirements.  
 
Councilor Mallar  asked whether federal funding involvement for building projects has 
requirements that differ from the new state requirement. Planning Officer Collette 
responded that staff has not found a federal funding requirement on minimum parking 
spaces per unit. 
 
Planning Officer Collette discussed the language changes in the City’s ordinance to align 
with state language.  
 
Councilor Carson moved to forward the proposed changes to the Land Development Code 
to full Council. Seconded by Councilor Faloon. Vote unless doubted, no doubt. 
 
 
3. Proposed Changes to Historic Preservation Code Process  
 
Chair Leonard introduced the agenda item. 
 
Planning Officer Collette presented on the proposed changes, such as  reducing 
affirmative votes required to a simple majority; allowing solar, generator, and heat pump 
installations, changing of awning fabric, and changes not visible from the street as minor 
revisions; lengthening the approval time period for Certificate of Appropriateness permits 
to 24 months; updating the requirements of replacement on deteriorated materials; 
clarifying that replacing to match is exempt; providing clarification on one of the hardship 
provisions r egarding contractor availability and extending timelines; and providing 
clarification on the application requirements for Certificate of Appropriateness.  
 
Councilor Mallar asked if these changes have been reviewed by the Historic Preservation 
Commission – Planning Officer Collette confirmed. Councilor Mallar noted that after 
discussing with the director, they had not completed it. Planning Officer asked if he meant 
the state response, and clarified that the City’s Commission has reviewed it, but the state 
has not yet. 
 
 
4. Request for Letter of Support on Maine Climate Superfund Bill 
 
Chair Leonard introduced the agenda item. 
 
Planning Officer Collette discussed the state bill pending to create a Climate Superfund, 
which would operate similarly to the federal superfund bill. She shared the intention to 
have polluters pay to clean up their pollution and analyze climate damages that Maine has 
experienced. Collette discussed Bangor’s vulnerabilities , such as flooding and severe 
storms, and the cost caused on infrastructure. She noted that the fund would allocate
compensatory fees that are recouped from companies to communities like Bangor to 
improve infrastructure. Collette expressed that staff requests a letter of support for the bill. 
 
Councilor Faloon asked how the fund would operate differently from Federal Emergency 
Management Agency (FEMA)  money. Planning Officer Collette responded that while 
FEMA money helps repair after disaster, the superfund would support increasing 
resilience on top of repairs.  
 
Councilor Carson moved to forward the request for a letter of support on the Maine Climate 
Superfund Bill to full Council. Seconded by Councilor Faloon. Roll call vote conducted –  
one opposed (Councilor Mallar), four in favor (Councilors Deane, Carson, Fal oon, 
Leonard). Motion passed. 
 
 
5. Staff Followup 
 A. Properties Covered in the Economic Development Fund 
 
Chair Leonard introduced the agenda item. 
 
Community & Economic Development Director Krieg discussed the use of the Economic 
Development Fund and why communities have enterprise funds. She presented a list of 
properties that fall within the fund. 
 
Councilor Mallar asked whether the utilities that are being payed on these leases include 
electricity. Development Assistant Maquillan responded that it depends on the lease terms 
that were set up at time of signing, and that there is currently one leased property with a 
tenant that the department is covering the electric cost for. She discussed that the lease 
was structured so that the rent due would cover the cost of all utilities. Councilor Mallar 
asked how long the department has had this lease –  Maquillan responded it was last 
amended in 2023.  
 
Councilor Mallar  asked follow up questions surrounding what the lease covers. 
Development Assistant Maquillan shared that when analyzing lease revenue versus what 
has been spent on each of the properties over the last five years, money has not been 
lost on any of them, and the department has more than broken even on all of the 
properties. Mallar expressed that breaking even is not a profitable operation and the City 
needs to make  money on the properties. Maquillan clarified that the properties have 
generated revenue. Community & Economic Development Director Krieg discussed that 
the Economic Development team is analyzing the leases to bring them to market rate. 
Mallar asked what percentage are at market rate now  – Chair Leonard added that he 
would like a defined performance metric or annual report in the future. Maquillan asked 
for clarification of what should be included in the report – Leonard responded a 
categorized list of the properties and annual revenue.  
 
Councilor Carson noted he would like more detail outside of the budget season for 
discussion on how to grow the enterprise fund, and asked what plans are with vacant 
buildings. Community & Economic Development Director Krieg responded that the 
Economic Development team works with potential tenants to lease vacant properties.  
 
Councilor Faloon asked if it is typical for municipalities to have a similar fund, whether 
other municipalities generate more revenue with them, and if so, what it is being used for. 
Community & Economic Development Director Krieg responded that it is unusual overall 
for a municipality to own this quantity of properties, which led to the creation of the fund
for maintenance, selling, and leasing of properties. Councilor Carson discussed a 
preference for not selling the properties, and rather leasing them.  
 
 
6. General Updates 
 A. Grandview Development 
 B. Maine Downtown Center Affiliate Program 
 
Chair Leonard introduced the agenda item. 
 
Community & Economic Development Director Krieg discussed the Grandview Avenue 
project, including location and affordability metrics . She shared potential site 
considerations with the development plan and the timeline for a formal presentation of the 
development plan.  
 
Councilor Mallar asked what the City will gain from it and whether there will be revenue 
from taxes – Krieg responded yes, since it will be privately owned. Councilor Mallar asked 
if the property cost them – Krieg responded that the development agreement outlined 
giving the property to the developer.  
 
Councilor Deane asked what the anticipated timeline is for breaking ground -- Community 
& Economic Development Director Krieg responded they are looking within the year. 
Councilor Faloon asked what the anticipated completion date is – Krieg responded that it 
will likely be completed in phases. Krieg discussed completing the rentals first to begin 
generating income.  
 
Community & Economic Development Director Krieg discussed that Bangor’s downtown 
will now be apart of the Maine Downtown Center Affiliate Program, sharing that it opens 
up funding abilities and the ability to market Bangor. 
 
Meeting adjourned at 8:25 P.M.

1. Floor Area Ratio Removal from Downtown Development District (DDD)  
 
Chair Carson introduced the agenda item. 
 
Planning Officer Collette described Floor Area Ratio (FAR), explaining it  is the floor area 
of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot.  She discussed the FAR of 
prominent buildings downtown to provide context. Collette described the proposal to 
remove the FAR dimensional control from the Downtown Development District (DDD) to 
increase flexibility for developers downtown and align with policies encouraging 
development and increased housing supply in the Comprehensive Plan.  
 
Councilor Faloon asked if there is a maximum height – Planning Officer Collette 
responded not downtown. Faloon  asked if having a maximum height could serve as a 
replacement to the FAR requirements due to potential impacts on downtown –  Collette 
noted it is a good policy discussion to have, and discussed the Historic Preservation 
Commission’s role in preservation downtown. Collette discussed the proposal in the new 
code to not have maximum heights, except for developments within a certain distance to 
residential districts.  
 
Councilor Deane asked what the tallest building downtown is currently – Planning Officer 
Collette responded likely the Camden National Bank with seven to eight stories. Collette 
discussed the height and setback requirements in various zones. 
 
Councilor Fish asked if the change  is intended for development, housing, or both –  
Planning Officer Collette responded any type of development.  
 
Councilor Beck expressed that other processes, such as Planning Board, would prevent 
the Council from worrying about skyscrapers. Planning Officer Collette discussed that 
most developments downtown will have to go to the Historic Preservation Commission. 
Collette discussed that if a building outside of the historic districts met all code 
requirements, a developer hypothetically could propose a skyscraper, but staff has not 
seen a demand for skyscrapers. Beck expressed that he believes eliminating FAR is a 
good step, and he would like to have a further conversation about potential height limits.
Councilor Mallar asked when to expect the completion of the Comprehensive Plan – 
Community & Economic Development Director Krieg clarified the Land Development Code 
updates. Planning Officer Collette responded late next year. Mallar  asked if it would be 
beneficial to wait to have the  discussion along with the code updates. Krieg responded 
that there is a project downtown awaiting the FAR change in order to proceed. Councilor 
Fish asked if height limitations could have exceptions with approval. Krieg discussed the 
creation of a special permit process where there is an allowed height, and anything 
additional would require a Conditional Use permit.  
 
Councilor Beck expressed interest in hearing from the Fire Department in conversations 
surrounding height.  
 
Planning Officer Collette asked if the Committee would like staff to incorporate a height 
limit with the ordinance change. Chair Carson expressed he is not in favor of adding a 
height limit and would like to see more data, and he would like to engage the Fire 
Department and Bangor International Airport in the conversation.  
 
Councilor Faloon moved to forward staff recommendation to full Council. Seconded by 
Councilor Fish. Vote unless doubted, no doubt.  
 
 
2. Discuss Proposed New Planning Fees 
 
Chair Carson introduced the agenda item. 
 
Planning Officer Collette discussed the proposed fees, including mailing and stormwater 
permitting fees.  
 
Councilor Faloon moved to forward staff recommendation to full Council. Seconded by 
Councilor Beck. 
 
 
3. Discuss Proposed Climate Rebate Program for Residents  
 
Chair Carson introduced the agenda item. 
 
Planning Officer Collette discussed the proposed program, which would utilize Climate 
Action Funds intended to implement the Penobscot Climate Action Plan. She discussed 
that helping residents retrofit their homes would be one of the highest impact toolkits, as 
buildings make up the largest contributor of greenhouse gas emissions in the City. Collette 
noted it has high potential to help residents increase resilience to power outages and high 
fuel costs.  
 
Planning Officer Collette discussed the proposal to use $50,000 from the Climate Action 
Fund to provide rebates on weatherization, heat pumps, and possibly solar. She explained 
that the rebates would work in concert with existing rebates from Efficiency Maine and 
Community Development Block Grants to provide fap financing. She discussed the 
structure of the potential rebate program, such as tiering the rebate to provide greater 
benefit to lower income households. Collette discussed the potential of incorpor ating 
energy audits for households. 
 
Councilor Fish discussed that solar installation may use a large portion of the funds due 
to cost. She noted the usefulness of energy audits. Fish discussed that bikes may not fit
into the category, as many elderly residents need energy efficiency in different avenues. 
Planning Officer Collette noted limiting this program to home heating upgrades. Collette 
discussed exploring rebates for plug- in solar to address the cost concerns and help 
renters.  
 
Chair Carson asked about using a portion of the funds to assist residents in obtaining the 
item that would be rebated to eliminate barriers. Planning Officer Collette discussed how 
Efficiency Maine’s process includes contractors taking the rebate into account and 
submitting paperwork for reimbursement, so the cost is taken off at the beginning. She 
expressed that staff will work with Efficiency Maine and contractors to explore how to  
incorporate a similar process.  
 
Councilor Mallar asked how much money is in the Climate Action Plan – Planning Officer 
Collette responded that it is pending, but it should be around $200,000.  
 
Councilor Faloon moved staff recommendation for the proposed climate rebate program 
for residents. Seconded by Councilor Fish.

This Order will authorize the City Manager to execute a subcontract with Northern Light Mayo Hospital in the amount of 
$468,197 to provide substance use and tobacco prevention services, and healthy eating active living promotion services 
in Piscataquis County as part of the Maine Prevention Network for FY 27 and 28. 
 
Bangor Public Health and Community Services is the lead agency for the project and provides substance use and tobacco 
prevention services, and healthy eating active living promotion services, in Penobscot County. Northern Light Mayo 
Hospital has been contracted to provide prevention services in Piscataquis County since January 1, 2023.
 
Resolve 26-236 authorizing the City Manager to accept and appropriate the Maine Prevention Network funding for FY27

Summary 
 
This Ordinance amendment would remove Floor Area Ratio (FAR) from the Downtown Development District 
(DDD) to provide flexibility for growth in downtown and promote infill development. Floor area ratio is the 
floor area of a building on a lot divided by the horizontal area of the lot. 
 
FAR was used to control building bulk and volume in the early to mid-20th century. When FARs were 
implemented around the country, some of the perceived benefits were protecting sunlight, neighborhood 
character, and infrastructure capacity, most of which do not hold true today. Additionally, some of the most 
well-known historic buildings downtown already exceed this standard. For example, the Graham Building 
where the Rudman Winchell offices are located have a FAR of approximately 4.5 and the Eastern Trust 
building at 6 State Street has a FAR of about 5.3. 
 
The proposed amendments align with policy recommendations 1 and 7 in the 2022 Comprehensive Plan 
regarding encouraging development in the growth boundary and increasing housing supply downtown by 
revising zoning regulations.

This Order will accept and appropriate up to $6,000 from Johns Hopkins University as partners on a National 
Institutes for Health (NIH) ARISE grant to increase access to PrEP.
 
For the past year, Bangor Public Health and Community Services has been exploring opportunities to expand 
access to Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP). PrEP is an effective medication to prevent the transmission of HIV. 
The current HIV outbreak has revealed gaps in access to PrEP. It is often not offered through traditional 
primary care. As a result, other delivery models need to be established. Bangor Public Health and Community 
Services currently has two clinic locations that could offer PrEP services. In addition to meeting a community 
need, this would also be a billable service to contribute to the Department's revenue.
 
The NIH ARISE grant will bring together Johns Hopkins University's expertise and leadership with Bangor 
Public Health and Community Service's on the ground experience to create a plan to include increase access to
 PrEP though community partnerships and system building. The funding will be used to off set staff time to 
work on developing the plan and expenses for supporting community meeting logistics.
